chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
title: Robert Mavouzy, the Guadeloupean saxophonist
summary: Mavouzy, from Guadeloupe, was another Charlie Parker who could just hear notes; he played in Butler's band, and Butler recalls the confusion about his being American. Butler then remarks that musicians are jealous of each other, more so now in New York.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players

blocks.x: So, Big Boy, and they worked together. This saxaphone player that I will tell you about later, Robert

MaVumzie (phonetic). MaVumzie was another Charlie Parker, see. He could just hear the notes and he would put them on you, too. He would put them right on you. And he wouldn't be ashamed. You see, we won the prize of France two times but, he didn't take care of his business.
He was from Guadeloupe). That is a sister island of Martinique.
Was he a man of color?
Oh, yes, just like you and I.In fact, we have the same ways, same everything.
Did you get to know him well?

Oh, yes, I liked him because he played in my band. I liked him very much. In fact, they thought that I was -- I always got hung up with them -- and when I brought that Cadillac over there, one of them said come on, get in the car -- naw, I ain't gonna get in it. I said, come on -- I thought you was from Guadalupe and you from America. And that's what happened.
No -- that's a thing that happens you know.
Oh, yes. Well now, it is here too now but before it wasn't here.
You mean here in New York?

The musicians are jealous of each other now. In fact, they are more ugly than most people will ever be, because they know a man can play, and they or he's a junkie, will say he can't play/ they do harm.
